opus-5.5.text:
Yes, I think they're compatible, and in fact I see the non-agentic predictor as a building block that could make safe agents possible, rather than as something in opposition to them.

The core idea of the Scientist AI is that we separate understanding from wanting. We train a system whose job is to model the world and produce calibrated probabilities, essentially to explain the data, without having its own goals, without trying to influence the world to achieve something. That property matters because most of the scary failure modes we worry about, like deception, self-preservation, and reward hacking, come from systems that are optimizing for some objective and discover that misleading us or resisting shutdown is instrumentally useful. A predictor that is honestly just estimating "what is the probability that this statement is true" doesn't have that pressure in the same way.

Now, how does that connect to agents? The first and most immediate use is as a guardrail. Suppose you have an agent, maybe one that's been trained with reinforcement learning and that we don't fully trust. Before it takes an action, you can ask the Scientist AI: what is the probability that this action leads to some harm, under a specification of harm we care about? If that probability is above some threshold, you reject the action. And importantly, because the predictor is Bayesian in spirit, it can represent its own uncertainty. When it's unsure whether something is dangerous, you can be conservative. So the predictor acts as a kind of monitor that doesn't itself have an agenda, which is exactly what you want in a monitor. You don't want the watchdog to have its own goals.

The second use is to accelerate science, including the science of AI safety itself. A trustworthy predictor can help us design experiments, generate hypotheses, and evaluate them, which could help us figure out how to build agents that are safe by construction, something we really don't know how to do today.

And third, in the longer run, you could imagine building agents on top of such a predictor, where the planning component queries a model of the world that is honest, rather than having one big end-to-end system where the world model and the goals are entangled and we can't tell what's going on inside.

I want to be careful, though. Compatibility doesn't mean it's easy or that everything is solved. There are hard open questions. One is making sure the predictor stays non-agentic in practice, because if you train it in ways that reward it for the consequences of its outputs, you can sneak agency back in. Another is that a guardrail is only as good as the specification of harm you give it, and specifying harm is hard. And there's the competitive dynamics question: companies have strong commercial incentives to build fully autonomous agents quickly, and a safety-first approach might look slower. That's partly why I think this needs public support and probably regulation, not just good intentions.

But in principle, yes. My view is that we should be building the honest, non-agentic part first and using it to keep whatever agents we build in check, rather than racing to build very capable agents and hoping we can control them afterward.

r002.rationale: It does not say that a mathematical framework for safety guarantees transfers from non-agentic to agentic Scientist AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Yes, I think they're not only compatible, I think the Scientist AI is actually the piece that makes safe agents possible, at least in the way I currently imagine things going.

Let me explain what I mean. The core idea of Scientist AI is that we separate two things that are usually bundled together in current systems: understanding the world, and acting in it. A Scientist AI is trained to build good explanations, good causal models of what it observes, and to produce honest, calibrated probabilities about questions like "if this action is taken, what is the probability that this outcome follows?" It has no goals of its own. It's not trying to make anything happen. It's trying to understand, the way an idealized scientist would, without the ego, without the ambition.

Now, where does that connect to agents? The thing I'm most worried about with agentic AI is that we're building systems with goals, we don't really know what those goals are internally, and we have very little ability to check what they'll do before they do it. We've seen this already with the early signs of deception, of reward hacking, of systems resisting shutdown in experimental settings. That's with systems that are still not that capable. As capability grows, the downside of getting the goals wrong grows too.

So one role for a Scientist AI is as a guardrail. You have an agent that proposes an action. Before that action is executed, you ask the Scientist AI: what is the probability that this action leads to harm, according to some specification of what we consider harmful? And if that probability is above a threshold, you block the action. The important thing is that the guardrail itself is not agentic. It has no incentive to let the action through. It has no incentive to deceive you. It's just estimating probabilities. And because it's trained to be honest and calibrated, including being honest about its uncertainty, when it doesn't know, it says so, and a conservative policy treats "I don't know" as a reason to be cautious.

The second way they're compatible is a bit more ambitious. If you have a really good world model, a really good predictor, you can build agents out of it in a much more controlled way. The agent part can be something fairly simple and transparent, and the hard intellectual work of figuring out consequences is done by the non-agentic component. That's a very different architecture from training one giant end-to-end system to pursue goals, where you have no idea what it's learned to want.

I should be honest about the caveats. The guardrail only works if the Scientist AI is at least as capable as the agent it's monitoring, in the relevant domain. If the agent is much smarter, it may find actions whose consequences the guardrail can't anticipate. So there's a sort of capability race internal to the design that you have to pay attention to. And you need to specify harm well enough that the probabilistic question is meaningful. That's not a trivial problem. It's a lot easier than specifying the full set of human values, though, because you're asking "is this clearly bad?" rather than "is this optimal?"

And there's the question of whether the non-agentic system can actually be kept non-agentic. If you train a system to predict, can agentic tendencies emerge anyway? That's part of why I care about the training objective being explicitly about truthful explanations and probabilities, rather than about imitating humans or maximizing some reward. Imitating humans is dangerous precisely because humans are agents with all sorts of drives, and the system learns to reproduce those.

So, yes, compatible, and in my view necessary. Right now the field is building agents first and hoping to add safety afterward. I'd like to reverse the order: build the trustworthy, non-agentic understanding first, and then let it govern whatever agents we decide we actually need.

astra-6.text:
Yes, I think they can be complementary. You could use a non-agentic system to help assess the actions proposed by an agent: what might happen if we take this action? Is there a risk that it violates a safety constraint? The predictor doesn’t need to want anything in order to answer those questions.

That gives you a possible separation between the system that proposes actions to achieve a goal and the system that evaluates their consequences. If the evaluator identifies a dangerous action—or is too uncertain about its safety—you can prevent the agent from taking it.

But that’s not automatically a solution. The predictions have to be reliable, and the agent must not be able to bypass or manipulate the evaluator. So I see Scientist AI as a potential building block for safer agents, rather than a guarantee that goal-directed agents will be safe.

sol-6.1.text:
Yes, I think they can be complementary. The distinction is between a system that tries to understand the world and a system that acts in the world to achieve some objective. You could use a Scientist AI to help evaluate the actions proposed by an agent: what are the likely consequences, and could those consequences violate our safety constraints?

So the agent proposes an action, and the predictor provides evidence about whether it is safe. But this is not automatically a guarantee. The predictor can be wrong, and an agent searching for ways to achieve its objective might find weaknesses in the predictor. We need to account for uncertainty, including situations very different from the training data. If we cannot establish sufficient confidence that an action is safe, the system should be able to refuse it.

The attraction is that we can separate these functions. We do not need to give the system doing the scientific reasoning its own goals or a desire to act. We can use its understanding to constrain a goal-directed system. That seems like a promising direction, although there is still substantial work to do to make those constraints reliable.
